prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the episodes to focal epilepsy, migraine or a functional disorder without vessel imaging: neck trauma and neck tenderness in a young patient with a focal deficit point to cervical artery dissection.
Do not give IV thrombolysis: she had an ischaemic stroke 2 weeks ago (subacute left pallidal infarct), and thrombolysis within 3 months of a prior ischaemic stroke may be harmful.

Do not start or restart antihypertensive treatment in the first 48 to 72 hours for blood pressure below 220/120 mmHg in a patient who receives neither IV thrombolysis nor thrombectomy and has no comorbid indication; it does not prevent death or dependency (AHA/ASA 2026, COR 3: No Benefit).
Do not continue oestrogen-containing contraception after this ischaemic stroke.
Do not start prophylactic antiseizure medication after the stroke without confirmed recurrent seizures.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (the start of today's episode, about 2 hours before arrival; the episode 2 weeks ago resolved completely) and the NIHSS (2: facial palsy 1, language 1, with right grip 4/5 and fine motor slowing that the scale does not capture).
Obtain non-contrast CT head first to exclude intracranial haemorrhage before any reperfusion decision.
Image the cervical and intracranial vessels (CTA head and neck) in this young patient with recent neck trauma and left neck tenderness.

IV thrombolysis: do not give. The episode 2 weeks ago was an ischaemic stroke (the subacute left pallidal infarct on CT), and IV thrombolysis within 3 months of a prior ischaemic stroke may be harmful; today's deficit is also mild (NIHSS 2) and was already improving. Neither the extracranial ICA dissection nor the tonic posturing at onset would by itself have excluded thrombolysis. Thrombectomy: not indicated (no large vessel occlusion; NIHSS below 6).

Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours; avoid hypotension and dehydration given the greater than 70% stenosis and the border-zone infarct.

Start antithrombotic therapy now, once CT has excluded haemorrhage, for the extracranial left ICA dissection and continue it for at least 3 months: aspirin (clopidogrel if aspirin is not tolerated) or anticoagulation, which CADISS and TREAT-CAD did not show to differ clearly; repeat vessel imaging at 3 to 6 months.

Stop the combined oral contraceptive permanently (oestrogen after ischaemic stroke is MEC category 4) and offer an intrauterine device or progestin-only method; recheck TSH 6 to 8 weeks after stopping it (TSH 5.8 on levothyroxine 50 mcg).

Treat the tonic hand episodes as possible acute symptomatic focal seizures or hemodynamic limb-shaking episodes: obtain prolonged EEG if they recur and start antiseizure medication only if recurrent seizures are confirmed.
Avoid contact sports and neck-loading activity until follow-up imaging shows healing of the dissection.

Start atorvastatin 80 mg daily: LDL 108 mg/dL after a non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke without known coronary disease meets the AHA/ASA 2021 secondary prevention indication (COR 1, SPARCL), although the mechanism is the carotid dissection rather than atherosclerosis; target LDL below 70 mg/dL; statins are avoided in pregnancy, so pair it with effective non-oestrogen contraception.

Seizure or hemodynamic limb-shaking episodes are a manifestation of the dissection, not an alternative to it.

key_clinical_evidence: A direct volleyball impact to the left neck 3 weeks earlier, left neck tenderness and two left-hemisphere events in a 28-year-old make cervical artery dissection the leading mechanism; vessel imaging of the neck is the decisive test.

CTA shows the left ICA dissection from C2 to the skull base (intimal flap, mural haematoma, greater than 70% stenosis) without intradural extension, so it is extracranial and would not by itself contraindicate IV thrombolysis.

Two infarcts of different ages in the same hemisphere (late subacute left pallidal infarct from the episode 2 weeks ago, acute left MCA-ACA border-zone infarct today) fit artery-to-artery embolism and hypoperfusion distal to a severe dissection.

NIHSS 2 (facial palsy 1, language 1) understates the dominant-hand deficit, but IV thrombolysis is not given: the episode 2 weeks ago was an ischaemic stroke (subacute left pallidal infarct on CT and MRI), and thrombolysis within 3 months of a prior ischaemic stroke may be harmful; antithrombotic therapy starts at once.

Tonic hand posturing before the deficit can be an acute symptomatic focal seizure from the ischaemic cortex or a hemodynamic limb-shaking episode; neither excludes stroke, and the EEG shows focal slowing without definite epileptiform discharges.

Connective tissue disease is assessed clinically: normal habitus, no skin hyperextensibility or atrophic scars, Beighton 3/9 and no family history; genetic testing is not indicated after a dissection with a clear traumatic trigger.
Combined oestrogen-containing contraception is unacceptable after ischaemic stroke and must be replaced.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC and coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG and troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA does not wait for creatinine.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Sofia Delgado is a 28-year-old right-handed woman who presents to the emergency department after experiencing a second episode of involuntary right hand clenching followed by transient difficulty with speech and fine motor movements in her right hand. Today's episode occurred approximately 2 hours prior to arrival while she was studying at home. She noted a sudden involuntary tonic posturing of her right hand lasting approximately 30 seconds, followed by difficulty typing on her laptop and mild slurring of her speech that persisted for roughly 15 minutes before gradually improving. She reports a similar but briefer episode approximately 2 weeks ago while at volleyball practice, which she initially attributed to muscle cramps and fatigue and did not seek medical attention. Notably, approximately 3 weeks prior to today's presentation, she sustained a direct impact to the left side of her neck from a volleyball during practice. She experienced mild neck pain and stiffness for a few days afterward but did not seek medical evaluation as the pain resolved with over-the-counter analgesics. She denies any headache, visual changes, nausea, vomiting, loss of consciousness, or generalized seizure activity during either episode. She has no history of seizures or epilepsy. She denies any recent febrile illness, weight loss, night sweats, skin rashes, or joint pain. She has not traveled recently and has no history of trauma other than the volleyball incident. Her partner, who witnessed today's episode, confirms the description and notes that she appeared fully conscious throughout, though she seemed frustrated by her difficulty speaking. The patient is particularly concerned because she needs full use of her right hand for laboratory work in her graduate program.
